quote: teach = def + hook (94 words); stem: Which term is defined as: The coefficient of dissociation (also written Ki, Ka) ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 7 (teach over ~90 words); item 4 (stem gives the answer away: 'coefficient of dissociation' names the term 'Kd (dissociation constant)')
fix: def:'The drug concentration that binds 50% of the available binding sites (also written Ki, Ka). From the law of mass action it equals K2/K1, the rate of dissociation over the rate of association. The smaller it is, the greater the affinity: inversely proportional.' hook:'Read on the x-axis of a binding curve; it says nothing about effect. Convert units before comparing (milli 10^-3, micro 10^-6, nano 10^-9): “the units ... about 10% of you are gonna miss it.”'

quote: teach = def + hook (98 words); def: Potency = EC50 or ED50: how much drug is needed ... the Day 1 slide lists tissue sensitivity, receptor number, receptor activity, affinity and efficacy.
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 7; transcript 9/24: "potency is not only going to be defined by the efficacy of the affinity, but also the tissue"
fix: def:'How much drug is needed for a given response, measured by the EC50 or ED50 and read on the x-axis (further left = more potent). It is a combination of affinity, efficacy and the tissue (number of receptors).'

quote: Which term is defined as: EC50: the effective concentration that produces 50% of a drug’s maximal response (in vitro). ED50: the effective dose ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4: the stem names the answer
fix: def:'The effective concentration (in vitro) or effective dose (in vivo) that produces 50% of a drug’s maximal response: the indicator of potency. The smaller it is, the greater the potency (inversely proportional).'

quote: Which term is defined as: The plateau of the dose–response curve (ceiling of effect) ... The height of Emax reflects efficacy
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The plateau of the dose–response curve (ceiling of effect), reached either because all receptors are occupied or because the physiological system has maxed out. Its height reflects efficacy.'

quote: Which term is defined as: Surmountable: an antagonist that the agonist can overcome ... Insurmountable: cannot be overcome ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The pair of names for whether an agonist can overcome an antagonist by increasing its concentration: yes when the antagonist binds and comes off (competitive = reversible), no when it binds irreversibly (irreversible = nonequilibrium-competitive = non-competitive).'

quote: Which term is defined as: Symmetrical shifts: successive rightward shifts of equal size ... Asymmetrical shifts: shifts of unequal size ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'Equal steps between successive curves come from increasing doses of an orthosteric competitor (competitive antagonist, inverse agonist, irreversible antagonist), because a tenfold increase in one drug needs a tenfold increase in the other; unequal steps come from allosteric agonists and antagonists, whose binding at the other site does not depend on the agonist.'

quote: Which term is defined as: ... TI = LD50/ED50 ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'An estimate of a drug’s margin of safety from quantal data: the ratio of the toxic (lethal or sub-lethal) effect to the therapeutic effect, LD50/ED50. A statement of how selective a drug is in producing a desired effect. The larger the ratio, the safer the drug.'

quote: Which term is defined as: SI = LD1/ED99: the dose that kills 1% of patients divided by the dose that treats 99% ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The dose that kills 1% of patients divided by the dose that treats 99% (LD1/ED99). For a drug to be safe the ED99 should be less than the LD1; the bigger the ratio, the safer. A large TI (1000) can hide a value of 0.1: 99 of 100 patients sleep and one dies.'

quote: Which term is defined as: On a cumulative quantal curve, the ED50 is the dose ... and the LD50 the dose ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'On a cumulative quantal curve, the dose of the drug that protects (treats) 50% of the population and the dose that kills 50% of the population. The lethal curve lies to the right of the effective curve; their ratio is the therapeutic index.'

quote: Which term is defined as: Receptor activity that is present by itself ... Receptors that have constitutive activity are more sensitive to inverse agonists
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'Receptor activity that is present by itself, without any drug, hormone or neurotransmitter (a baseline above 0%). Receptors that have it are more sensitive to inverse agonists; it is what an inverse agonist shuts down.'

quote: Which term is defined as: The potency seen in vivo ... It is “apparent” because ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The potency seen in vivo, where pharmacokinetics (age, absorption, distribution, elimination, drug–drug interactions) determines how much drug reaches the site of action; it is not the total concentration of the drug that acts. A DRC built in vivo (ED50) shows it.'

quote: Which term is defined as: The three α subunit types to know. Gαs (stimulation) activates adenylate cyclase ... Gαi ... Gαq ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The three α subunit types to know: one (stimulation) activates adenylate cyclase and increases cAMP (β1 in the heart, ↑HR); one (inhibition) inhibits adenylate cyclase and decreases cAMP (M2 in the heart, ↓HR; α2 in the CNS); one activates phospholipase C, which converts PIP2 to IP3 and releases Ca++ from the ER (α1 in smooth muscle).'

quote: Which term is defined as: Two atoms share a pair of electrons ... Covalent binding is called irreversible, insurmountable or non-competitive ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'Two atoms share a pair of electrons; the bond cannot be broken at body temperature and gives a long duration of action. Drugs that bind this way are called irreversible, insurmountable or non-competitive, three names for one property; ionic, hydrogen and van der Waals bonds are reversible, surmountable, competitive.'

quote: Which term is defined as: An antagonist held by reversible bonds ... reversible, surmountable and competitive are three names for the same property ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'An antagonist held by ionic, hydrogen or van der Waals bonds: it competes with the agonist for the orthosteric pocket, binds and comes off, and can be outcompeted by more agonist (the agonist still reaches its Emax). Example: prazosin at α1.'

quote: Which term is defined as: An antagonist that binds by a covalent bond, so once bound it does not come off at body temperature: irreversible, insurmountable, non-competitive ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'An antagonist that binds by a covalent bond, so once bound it does not come off at body temperature and the agonist cannot outcompete it. It has the highest affinity (smallest Kd). Example: phenoxybenzamine (α1 and α2).'

quote: Which term is defined as: The receptor’s own binding pocket ... Orthosteric drugs (phenylephrine, prazosin, phenoxybenzamine at α1) compete ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'The receptor’s own binding pocket, where the endogenous agonist binds. Drugs that bind there (phenylephrine, prazosin, phenoxybenzamine at α1) compete for that one pocket, so only one can be bound at a time: either one or the other, not both.'

quote: Which term is defined as: A different (allotopic) binding site on the receptor. An allosteric drug binds there ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'A different (allotopic) binding site on the receptor. A drug binding there can increase or decrease the affinity and/or efficacy of another drug for the receptor, or have no effect; it does not compete for the orthosteric pocket, so both drugs can be bound at once.'

quote: Which term is defined as: An enzyme, ion channel or transport protein ... frequently the proximal effector protein is not the ultimate physiological target
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'An enzyme, ion channel or transport protein that creates, moves or degrades a small molecule or ions, e.g., adenylate cyclase (AC), phospholipase C (PLC). It amplifies the signal (his “factor system”) and is frequently not the ultimate physiological target.'

quote: Which term is defined as: A graph relating drug dose (DRC) or concentration (CRC) on the x-axis ...
source: REVIEW_BRIEF item 4
fix: def:'A graph relating drug dose or concentration on the x-axis (independent variable, log units, sigmoid curve) to the intensity of effect on the y-axis (dependent variable, normalized as % of maximum response). It is the model used to predict and compare drugs and determine potency.'

quote: Which term is defined as: The literature name for an allosteric antagonist: binds reversibly at another site in the receptor ... — options include Allosteric antagonist (confuse list)
source: Day 4 slide ~37: "Antagonist; Negative allosteric modulators (NAMs)" — the two names are one drug, so 'Allosteric antagonist' is also a defensible answer
fix: remove the `nam` term; fold the naming into allosteric-antagonist: term:'Allosteric antagonist (NAM)', hook:'Literature name: negative allosteric modulator (NAM); the allosteric agonist is the PAM. It does not compete for the orthosteric pocket; a competitive antagonist does. “As far as I know, all allosteric agonists and antagonists are reversible.”'

quote: Which term is defined as: A drug with no efficacy (ε = zero) and equal affinity for receptors in the active and inactive state ... Examples: prazosin (α1), metoprolol (β1). — options include Competitive (reversible) antagonist
source: Day 4 slide ~43: "Competitive Antagonist ... equal affinity for active and inactive states; R = Affinity = R* 'Neutral'; They Have Affinity, But No PCOL Efficacy" — he uses competitive antagonist and neutral for the same drug, so the distractor is defensible
fix: def:'The two-state description of the competitive antagonist: no efficacy (ε = zero) and equal affinity for receptors in the active and inactive state, so it occupies the receptor and keeps agonists from binding but does not change the balance of receptor states. Examples: prazosin (α1), metoprolol (β1).' and drop 'competitive-antagonist' from confuse

quote: Which term is defined as: The study of the interaction of drugs with biological systems ... — options include Pharmacodynamics (PD)

quote: Which term is defined as: A reduction in the total number of receptors in a cell or tissue over seconds, minutes, hours or days after prolonged exposure to an agonist ... — options include Long-term down-regulation (internalization)
source: Part 2 page 21: the receptor-number reduction is the long-term process (endocytosis, degradation); page 20 uses the same title for the umbrella. Either option fits the def
fix: def:'The umbrella for what the cell does after prolonged exposure to an agonist (too much stimulation): rapid desensitization, then a reduction in the total number of receptors. Analogous to an irreversible antagonist: fewer receptors, so the agonist becomes less potent (shift right) and may lose its maximal effect.'
